Purpose and architectural principles\n\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\nversioned HTTP API.\n\nThe design follows these principles:\n\n1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\n units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\n2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\n consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\n3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\n not independently entered totals.\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\n approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\n functionality is introduced.\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\n adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\n\n## 2. Current decisions and terminology\n\nThe approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\nagreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\ninternationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\n\n### Authentication provider clarification\n\nIssue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\nwas successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\n**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\nSupabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\nat the same time.\n\nAuthentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\n`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\nthe frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\nThe provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\nresolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\n\n## 3. High-level architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TB\n subgraph Clients[Clients]\n User[Browser user]\n Consumer[External API or dataset consumer]\n end\n\n subgraph Applications[Separate deployable applications]\n Frontend[React and Vite frontend]\n API[Handwritten Express API

current managed identity provider]\n External[External data or sports API
adapter and source provenance]\n\n subgraph Data[Persistent data]\n DB[(PostgreSQL
events, users, grants, statistics, audit)]\n Files[(Object storage
planned for uploads and exports)]\n end\n\n subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\n Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\n Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\n Cache[(Cache)]\n Live[Live event provider]\n Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\n end\n\n User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\n Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\n Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\n Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\n Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\n API -->|Verify access token| Auth\n API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\n API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\n API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\n API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\n Queue -.-> Worker\n Worker -.-> DB\n Worker -.-> Files\n API -.-> Cache\n Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\n Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\n Definitions -.-> Worker\n```\n\nSolid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\nIntermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\nshould store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\nIts provider has not yet been selected.\n\n### Trust boundaries\n\n- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\n- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\n rules, quotas, and audit logging.\n- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\n environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\n storage credentials remain server-side.\n- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\n privileges.\n- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\n asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\n\n## 4. Component responsibilities\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Delivery tier and state |\n|---|---|---|\n| React frontend (`apps/frontend`) | Render responsive and accessible search, dashboard, authentication, submission, review, and export journeys. Perform helpful client validation and send application data only to the backend. | Basic; application scaffold exists, product journeys are planned. |\n| Express backend (`apps/backend`) | Own `/api/v1`, authoritative validation, authentication middleware, role and scope checks, event ingestion, derivation orchestration, queries, exports, external integrations, audit logs, and safe error responses. | Basic; health and identity-proof endpoints exist, domain modules are planned. |\n| Shared contracts (`packages/contracts`) | Hold versioned request/response schemas and TypeScript types shared by the applications. It contains no secrets, database access, or authorisation decisions. | Basic; health contract exists and domain contracts are planned. |\n| Supabase Auth | Manage Google OAuth and future approved account lifecycle flows; issue tokens that the backend verifies. It proves identity only. | Basic; selected and backend verification is proved. |\n| Backend authorisation | Map the verified provider subject to `app_user`, enforce account status, application role, approved-submitter state, and scoped grants on every protected route. | Basic; model and middleware are planned. |\n| PostgreSQL | Store identity mappings, grants, reference data, submissions, immutable event revisions, review and correction history, statistic definitions/results, export metadata, and audit records. Enforce integrity with constraints and transactions. | Basic; hosted connection and event model are approved, full migrations are planned. |\n| Submission and validation service | Accept manual JSON and file submissions, identify duplicates, apply versioned structural and cricket-domain rules, normalise source data, and produce actionable validation results. | Basic. |\n| Derivation service | Calculate deterministic fixture, season, competition, and career statistics from accepted current event revisions; record the definition version and input provenance. | Basic for required statistics; versioned/custom definitions are Advanced. |\n| File and export service | Enforce upload type/size limits, calculate checksums, retain source provenance, create immutable release manifests, and provide authorised downloads. | Basic for small synchronous files; object storage and asynchronous large exports are Intermediate. |\n| External integration adapter | Isolate provider formats and credentials; apply timeouts, bounded retries, rate limits, schema validation, idempotency, and source/retrieval metadata. Cricsheet is the current historical file source; the required runtime external API is undecided. | Basic adapter and one integration required. |\n| Worker and job queue | Process large imports, recomputation, exports, and scheduled synchronisation outside request timeouts. Jobs are idempotent, retryable, observable, and dead-lettered after bounded failures. | Intermediate. |\n| Cache | Reduce repeated reads of published statistics and reference data. Cache entries are keyed by data and definition version and invalidated after accepted corrections or recalculation. | Intermediate; introduce only after measurement. |\n| Live ingestion adapter | Receive or poll live events, order and deduplicate them, handle late corrections, and pass them through the same validation and acceptance path as file submissions. | Advanced. |\n| Custom statistic engine | Store reviewed, versioned definitions and calculate results in a restricted expression model. It must not execute arbitrary user code or unbounded database queries. | Advanced. |\n| MkDocs site | Publish architecture, API, database, security, deployment, testing, methodology, and data-source documentation independently of the product applications. | Basic; deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages. |\n\n## 5. Authorisation model\n\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\nbe preserved.\n\n| Actor | Typical permissions |\n|---|---|\n| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\n| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\n| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\n| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\n| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\n\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\n\n```text\nverified identity\nAND active application account\nAND approved-submitter capability\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\nAND route-specific permission\n```\n\nThe target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\nscope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\n`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\n`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\nstate is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n actor User\n participant UI as React frontend\n participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n participant API as Express API\n participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n else Verified provider identity\n Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\n alt Account or permission check fails\n API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n else Route and resource scope allowed\n API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n API-->>UI: Safe response\n end\n end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n actor Submitter\n participant UI as Frontend or API client\n participant API as Handwritten API\n participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n participant Validate as Validation service\n participant DB as PostgreSQL\n participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n participant Files as File and export storage\n\n Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\n API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n opt Raw source file retained\n API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n end\n API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n alt Validation fails\n Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n else Valid but review required\n Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\\n+agreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\\n+internationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\\n+\\n+### Authentication provider clarification\\n+\\n+Issue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\\n+was successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\\n+**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\\n+Supabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\\n+at the same time.\\n+\\n+Authentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\\n+`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\\n+the frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\\n+The provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\\n+resolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\\n+\\n+## 3. planned for uploads and exports)]\\n+ end\\n+\\n+ subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\\n+ Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\\n+ Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\\n+ Cache[(Cache)]\\n+ Live[Live event provider]\\n+ Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\\n+ end\\n+\\n+ User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\\n+ Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\\n+ Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\\n+ Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\\n+ Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\\n+ API -->|Verify access token| Auth\\n+ API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\\n+ API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\\n+ API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\\n+ API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\\n+ Queue -.-> Worker\\n+ Worker -.-> DB\\n+ Worker -.-> Files\\n+ API -.-> Cache\\n+ Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\\n+ Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\\n+ Definitions -.-> Worker\\n+```\\n+\\n+Solid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\\n+Intermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\\n+should store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\\n+Its provider has not yet been selected.\\n+\\n+### Trust boundaries\\n+\\n+- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\\n+- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\\n+ rules, quotas, and audit logging.\\n+- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\\n+ environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\\n+ storage credentials remain server-side.\\n+- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\\n+ privileges.\\n+- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\\n+ asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\\n+\\n+## 4. Component responsibilities\\n+\\n+| Component | Responsibility | Delivery tier and state |\\n+|---|---|---|\\n+| React frontend (`apps/frontend`) | Render responsive and accessible search, dashboard, authentication, submission, review, and export journeys. Perform helpful client validation and send application data only to the backend. | Basic; application scaffold exists, product journeys are planned. |\\n+| Express backend (`apps/backend`) | Own `/api/v1`, authoritative validation, authentication middleware, role and scope checks, event ingestion, derivation orchestration, queries, exports, external integrations, audit logs, and safe error responses. | Basic; health and identity-proof endpoints exist, domain modules are planned. |\\n+| Shared contracts (`packages/contracts`) | Hold versioned request/response schemas and TypeScript types shared by the applications. It contains no secrets, database access, or authorisation decisions. | Basic; health contract exists and domain contracts are planned. |\\n+| Supabase Auth | Manage Google OAuth and future approved account lifecycle flows; issue tokens that the backend verifies. It proves identity only. | Basic; selected and backend verification is proved. |\\n+| Backend authorisation | Map the verified provider subject to `app_user`, enforce account status, application role, approved-submitter state, and scoped grants on every protected route. | Basic; model and middleware are planned. |\\n+| PostgreSQL | Store identity mappings, grants, reference data, submissions, immutable event revisions, review and correction history, statistic definitions/results, export metadata, and audit records. Enforce integrity with constraints and transactions. | Basic; hosted connection and event model are approved, full migrations are planned. |\\n+| Submission and validation service | Accept manual JSON and file submissions, identify duplicates, apply versioned structural and cricket-domain rules, normalise source data, and produce actionable validation results. | Basic. |\\n+| Derivation service | Calculate deterministic fixture, season, competition, and career statistics from accepted current event revisions; record the definition version and input provenance. | Basic for required statistics; versioned/custom definitions are Advanced. |\\n+| File and export service | Enforce upload type/size limits, calculate checksums, retain source provenance, create immutable release manifests, and provide authorised downloads. | Basic for small synchronous files; object storage and asynchronous large exports are Intermediate. |\\n+| External integration adapter | Isolate provider formats and credentials; apply timeouts, bounded retries, rate limits, schema validation, idempotency, and source/retrieval metadata. Cricsheet is the current historical file source; the required runtime external API is undecided. | Basic adapter and one integration required. |\\n+| Worker and job queue | Process large imports, recomputation, exports, and scheduled synchronisation outside request timeouts. Cache entries are keyed by data and definition version and invalidated after accepted corrections or recalculation. | Intermediate; introduce only after measurement. |\\n+| Live ingestion adapter | Receive or poll live events, order and deduplicate them, handle late corrections, and pass them through the same validation and acceptance path as file submissions. | Advanced. |\\n+| Custom statistic engine | Store reviewed, versioned definitions and calculate results in a restricted expression model. It must not execute arbitrary user code or unbounded database queries. | Advanced. |\\n+| MkDocs site | Publish architecture, API, database, security, deployment, testing, methodology, and data-source documentation independently of the product applications. | Basic; deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages. |\\n+\\n+## 5. Authorisation model\\n+\\n+The minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\\n+remain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\\n+be preserved.\\n+\\n+| Actor | Typical permissions |\\n+|---|---|\\n+| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\\n+| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\\n+| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\\n+| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\\n+| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\\n+| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\\n+\\n+An approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+verified identity\\n+AND active application account\\n+AND approved-submitter capability\\n+AND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\\n+AND route-specific permission\\n+```\\n+\\n+The target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\\n+scope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\\n+`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\\n+`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\\n+state is never an authorisation control.\\n+\\n+## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+sequenceDiagram\\n+ actor User\\n+ participant UI as React frontend\\n+ participant Auth as Supabase Auth\\n+ participant API as Express API\\n+ participant DB as PostgreSQL\\n+\\n+ User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\\n+ UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\\n+ Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\\n+ UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\\n+ API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\\n+ alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\\n+ API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\\n+ else Verified provider identity\\n+ Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\\n+ API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\\n+ alt Account or permission check fails\\n+ API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\\n+ else Route and resource scope allowed\\n+ API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\\n+ API-->>UI: Safe response\\n+ end\\n+ end\\n+```\\n+\\n+Important controls are:\\n+\\n+- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\\n+- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\\n+- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\\n+- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\\n+- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\\n+ if supported by the selected provider;\\n+- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\\n+ narrow administrative operations that require them; and\\n+- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\\n+\\n+## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\\n+\\n+### End-to-end flow\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+sequenceDiagram\\n+ actor Submitter\\n+ participant UI as Frontend or API client\\n+ participant API as Handwritten API\\n+ participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\\n+ participant Validate as Validation service\\n+ participant DB as PostgreSQL\\n+ participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\\n+ participant Files as File and export storage\\n+\\n+ Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\\n+ UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\\n+ API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\\n+ AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\\n+ API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\\n+ API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\\n+ opt Raw source file retained\\n+ API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\\n+ end\\n+ API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\\n+ alt Validation fails\\n+ Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\\n+ API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\\n+ else Valid but review required\\n+ Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\\n+ API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\\n+ else Accepted by policy or reviewer\\n+ Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\\n+ DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\\n+ Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\\n+ Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\\n+ Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\\n+ Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\\n+ API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\\n+ end\\n+```\\n+\\n+For the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\\n+derived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\\n+creation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\\n+event cannot exist without its recalculation job.\\n+\\n+### Validation layers\\n+\\n+1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\\n+ decompression limits.\\n+2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\\n+ policy.\\n+3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\\n+ player joins.\\n+4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\\n+ super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\\n+5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\\n+ duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\\n+6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\\n+7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\\n+ or needs an independent reviewer.\\n+\\n+Validation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\\n+queries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\\n+accepted records or none of them.\\n+\\n+### Corrections and derivation\\n+\\n+Delivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\\n+live revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\\n+reads only the approved current-event view.\\n+\\n+Required statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\\n+the event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\\n+non-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\\n+bowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\\n+\\n+Each stored result identifies:\\n+\\n+- statistic definition and version;\\n+- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\\n+- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\\n+- calculation status and timestamp; and\\n+- value and units.\\n+\\n+A correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\\n+cache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\\n+version.\\n+\\n+## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\\n+\\n+### Uploads and source artefacts\\n+\\n+- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\\n+- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\\n+ generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\\n+ SHA-256 checksums.\\n+- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\\n+ metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\\n+- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\\n+ determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\\n+- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\\n+ uploads are enabled.\\n+\\n+### Dataset exports\\n+\\n+Small filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\\n+return `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\\n+scope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\\n+provenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\\n+public releases may use stable public links.\\n+\\n+### External integration\\n+\\n+Cricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\\n+download and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\\n+runtime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\\n+value, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\\n+\\n+All providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\\n+submission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\\n+with jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\\n+observable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\\n+are retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\\n+not health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\\n+\\n+## 9. Basic, Intermediate, and Advanced evolution\\n+\\n+| Tier | Architecture need | Completion signal |\\n+|---|---|---|\\n+| Basic | Separate responsive frontend and handwritten versioned backend; PostgreSQL persistence; managed identity; backend roles and approved-submitter scopes; event/file submission; layered validation; traceable corrections; required derived statistics; one external integration; small exports; automated tests; CI/CD and public documentation. | A user can submit in-scope T20 events, see validation outcomes, and retrieve independently verified statistics and a documented dataset/API from deployed applications. |\\n+| Intermediate | Durable background jobs for batch ingestion, large recalculation and exports; object storage; job status and retries; caching of measured hot reads; richer review workflow; API credentials/quotas; observability, backup/restore, and performance testing. | Large real-data operations complete outside HTTP timeouts, survive retries without duplication, expose useful status, and meet agreed performance/recovery targets. |\\n+| Advanced | Live event ingestion and correction handling; versioned custom statistic definitions; dependency-aware incremental recomputation; safe expression limits; change feeds/release differences; stronger scaling and cache invalidation. | Live corrections converge on auditable results, and approved custom definitions calculate reproducibly without arbitrary code execution or unbounded resource use. |\\n+\\n+Promotion to a later tier is evidence-based. Batch processing is introduced when request-time\\n+work exceeds agreed limits; caching is introduced after profiling; live ingestion depends on a\\n+licensed reliable feed; and custom statistics depend on an approved safe definition model.\\n+\\n+## 10. Purpose and architectural principles\n\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\nversioned HTTP API.\n\nThe design follows these principles:\n\n1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\n units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\n2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\n consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\n3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\n not independently entered totals.\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\n approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\n functionality is introduced.\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\n adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\n\n## 2. Current decisions and terminology\n\nThe approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\nagreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\ninternationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\n\n### Authentication provider clarification\n\nIssue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\nwas successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\n**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\nSupabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\nat the same time.\n\nAuthentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\n`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\nthe frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\nThe provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\nresolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\n\n## 3. High-level architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TB\n subgraph Clients[Clients]\n User[Browser user]\n Consumer[External API or dataset consumer]\n end\n\n subgraph Applications[Separate deployable applications]\n Frontend[React and Vite frontend]\n API[Handwritten Express API
/api/v1]\n end\n\n Auth[Supabase Auth
current managed identity provider]\n External[External data or sports API
adapter and source provenance]\n\n subgraph Data[Persistent data]\n DB[(PostgreSQL
events, users, grants, statistics, audit)]\n Files[(Object storage
planned for uploads and exports)]\n end\n\n subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\n Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\n Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\n Cache[(Cache)]\n Live[Live event provider]\n Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\n end\n\n User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\n Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\n Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\n Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\n Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\n API -->|Verify access token| Auth\n API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\n API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\n API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\n API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\n Queue -.-> Worker\n Worker -.-> DB\n Worker -.-> Files\n API -.-> Cache\n Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\n Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\n Definitions -.-> Worker\n```\n\nSolid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\nIntermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\nshould store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\nIts provider has not yet been selected.\n\n### Trust boundaries\n\n- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\n- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\n rules, quotas, and audit logging.\n- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\n environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\n storage credentials remain server-side.\n- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\n privileges.\n- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\n asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\n\n## 4. Component responsibilities\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Delivery tier and state |\n|---|---|---|\n| React frontend (`apps/frontend`) | Render responsive and accessible search, dashboard, authentication, submission, review, and export journeys. Perform helpful client validation and send application data only to the backend. | Basic; application scaffold exists, product journeys are planned. |\n| Express backend (`apps/backend`) | Own `/api/v1`, authoritative validation, authentication middleware, role and scope checks, event ingestion, derivation orchestration, queries, exports, external integrations, audit logs, and safe error responses. | Basic; health and identity-proof endpoints exist, domain modules are planned. |\n| Shared contracts (`packages/contracts`) | Hold versioned request/response schemas and TypeScript types shared by the applications. It contains no secrets, database access, or authorisation decisions. | Basic; health contract exists and domain contracts are planned. |\n| Supabase Auth | Manage Google OAuth and future approved account lifecycle flows; issue tokens that the backend verifies. It proves identity only. | Basic; selected and backend verification is proved. |\n| Backend authorisation | Map the verified provider subject to `app_user`, enforce account status, application role, approved-submitter state, and scoped grants on every protected route. | Basic; model and middleware are planned. |\n| PostgreSQL | Store identity mappings, grants, reference data, submissions, immutable event revisions, review and correction history, statistic definitions/results, export metadata, and audit records. Enforce integrity with constraints and transactions. | Basic; hosted connection and event model are approved, full migrations are planned. |\n| Submission and validation service | Accept manual JSON and file submissions, identify duplicates, apply versioned structural and cricket-domain rules, normalise source data, and produce actionable validation results. | Basic. |\n| Derivation service | Calculate deterministic fixture, season, competition, and career statistics from accepted current event revisions; record the definition version and input provenance. | Basic for required statistics; versioned/custom definitions are Advanced. |\n| File and export service | Enforce upload type/size limits, calculate checksums, retain source provenance, create immutable release manifests, and provide authorised downloads. | Basic for small synchronous files; object storage and asynchronous large exports are Intermediate. |\n| External integration adapter | Isolate provider formats and credentials; apply timeouts, bounded retries, rate limits, schema validation, idempotency, and source/retrieval metadata. Cricsheet is the current historical file source; the required runtime external API is undecided. | Basic adapter and one integration required. |\n| Worker and job queue | Process large imports, recomputation, exports, and scheduled synchronisation outside request timeouts. Jobs are idempotent, retryable, observable, and dead-lettered after bounded failures. | Intermediate. |\n| Cache | Reduce repeated reads of published statistics and reference data. Cache entries are keyed by data and definition version and invalidated after accepted corrections or recalculation. | Intermediate; introduce only after measurement. |\n| Live ingestion adapter | Receive or poll live events, order and deduplicate them, handle late corrections, and pass them through the same validation and acceptance path as file submissions. | Advanced. |\n| Custom statistic engine | Store reviewed, versioned definitions and calculate results in a restricted expression model. It must not execute arbitrary user code or unbounded database queries. | Advanced. |\n| MkDocs site | Publish architecture, API, database, security, deployment, testing, methodology, and data-source documentation independently of the product applications. | Basic; deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages. |\n\n## 5. Authorisation model\n\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\nbe preserved.\n\n| Actor | Typical permissions |\n|---|---|\n| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\n| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\n| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\n| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\n| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\n\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\n\n```text\nverified identity\nAND active application account\nAND approved-submitter capability\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\nAND route-specific permission\n```\n\nThe target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\nscope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\n`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\n`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\nstate is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n actor User\n participant UI as React frontend\n participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n participant API as Express API\n participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n else Verified provider identity\n Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\n alt Account or permission check fails\n API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n else Route and resource scope allowed\n API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n API-->>UI: Safe response\n end\n end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n actor Submitter\n participant UI as Frontend or API client\n participant API as Handwritten API\n participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n participant Validate as Validation service\n participant DB as PostgreSQL\n participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n participant Files as File and export storage\n\n Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n API->>API: Enforce content type and size; calculate checksum\n API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n opt Raw source file retained\n API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n end\n API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n alt Validation fails\n Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n else Valid but review required\n Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9. It accepts\\n+traceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\\n+from those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\\n+versioned HTTP API.\\n+\\n+The design follows these principles:\\n+\\n+1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\\n+ units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\\n+2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\\n+ consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\\n+3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\\n+ not independently entered totals.\\n+4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\\n+ approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\\n+5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\\n+6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\\n+ functionality is introduced.\\n+7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\\n+ adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\\n+\\n+## 2. Current decisions and terminology\\n+\\n+The approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\\n+agreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\\n+internationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\\n+\\n+### Authentication provider clarification\\n+\\n+Issue #38 originally named **Firebase Authentication**. That was the selection in ADR-002 and\\n+was successfully prototyped, but ADR-004 superseded it. The repository now implements\\n+**Supabase Auth** with Google as the initial OAuth provider. The architecture therefore shows\\n+Supabase Auth as the current provider and does not propose running Firebase and Supabase Auth\\n+at the same time.\\n+\\n+Authentication remains behind a provider boundary. Application users are keyed by\\n+`(auth_provider, provider_subject)`, so a formally approved return to Firebase would replace\\n+the frontend SDK and backend token verifier without changing role, event, or statistic data.\\n+The provider discrepancy and the scope of the client's Supabase compliance approval must be\\n+resolved before production; see [Risks and unresolved decisions](#12-risks-and-unresolved-decisions).\\n+\\n+## 3. Authorisation model\\n+\\n+The minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\\n+remain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\\n+be preserved.\\n+\\n+| Actor | Typical permissions |\\n+|---|---|\\n+| Public viewer | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata. |\\n+| Registered user | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable. |\\n+| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\\n+| Reviewer | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events. |\\n+| Administrator | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited. |\\n+| API consumer | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default. |\\n+\\n+An approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+verified identity\\n+AND active application account\\n+AND approved-submitter capability\\n+AND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\\n+AND route-specific permission\\n+```\\n+\\n+The target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\\n+scope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\\n+`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\\n+`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\\n+state is never an authorisation control.\\n+\\n+## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\\n+\\n+```mermaid\\n+sequenceDiagram\\n+ actor User\\n+ participant UI as React frontend\\n+ participant Auth as Supabase Auth\\n+ participant API as Express API\\n+ participant DB as PostgreSQL\\n+\\n+ User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\\n+ UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\\n+ Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\\n+ UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\\n+ API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\\n+ alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\\n+ API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\\n+ else Verified provider identity\\n+ Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\\n+ API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\\n+ alt Account or permission check fails\\n+ API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\\n+ else Route and resource scope allowed\\n+ API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\\n+ API-->>UI: Safe response\\n+ end\\n+ end\\n+```\\n+\\n+Important controls are:\\n+\\n+- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\\n+- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\\n+- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\\n+- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\\n+- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\\n+ if supported by the selected provider;\\n+- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\\n+ narrow administrative operations that require them; and\\n+- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\\n+\\n+## 7. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\\n+accepted records or none of them.\\n+\\n+### Corrections and derivation\\n+\\n+Delivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\\n+live revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\\n+reads only the approved current-event view.\\n+\\n+Required statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. Build public frontend pages that allow anyone to browse competitions, seasons, fixtures, competitors and participants without signing in.

Published sport information and statistics are public. Authentication is required only for account functions and approved event submission.

Public competition and season browsing.

Event upload.
Administrator management.
Statistics visualisation beyond navigation placeholders.
Direct database or Supabase access from the frontend.

Public competition, fixture and participant read APIs.

Provide screenshots, frontend test output and the linked Pull Request.

Security
Do not render or request private account or submitter data.

Use semantic headings, labelled controls, visible focus and readable status messages.

Responsiveness
Layouts must adapt without overlapping or horizontal scrolling on common mobile widths.
